name: Kindling Spore Drift

detectability.signature: Organic compound signatures; bioluminescent emission in orange-red spectrum; thermal hotspots distributed irregularly throughout the cloud

proximity: Sensors detect a vast cloud of organic particulate matter with internal thermal hotspots reaching several hundred kelvin
Bioluminescent emissions create a diffuse orange-red glow throughout the cloud, visible as a warm smear against the starfield
Spore density increases toward the cloud interior, reducing visibility and sensor range
contact: Spores adhere to hull surfaces on contact, forming a thin biological film that begins metabolizing hull coatings and surface materials
Thermal output from metabolically active spore colonies on the hull creates localized heating
Air filtration systems, if exposed through docking or EVA, risk spore contamination of internal atmosphere
prolonged_exposure: Spore colonies on hull surfaces mature and produce exothermic metabolic byproducts that progressively corrode hull materials
Thermal output from mature colonies can reach temperatures sufficient to weaken structural alloys at contact points
If spores breach internal systems, they colonize any organic or carbon-based material, including wiring insulation, seals, and stored supplies, generating heat as they metabolize

behavior.cycle: The cloud migrates along a roughly elliptical path through the sector over an estimated 2,400-year orbital period; internal colony activity cycles between dormancy and active metabolism every 3-7 weeks

phenomena: The cloud glows with bioluminescent orange-red light produced by metabolically active spore colonies, creating an appearance resembling embers drifting through space
Thermal hotspots within the cloud mark locations of intense colonial metabolic activity, reaching temperatures of 400-700 kelvin
Dormant spores, when activated by contact with matter or energy, ignite into metabolic activity within minutes, visibly glowing as they consume available material
The cloud sheds dense tendrils of spore material that extend thousands of kilometers beyond the main body, slowly dispersing into the interstellar medium
hazards: Biological contamination of hull surfaces leading to progressive corrosion and structural weakening
Thermal damage from exothermic spore metabolism at colony maturation points on ship surfaces
Internal contamination risk if spores breach atmosphere seals, potentially compromising life support and stored materials
opportunities: Study of a space-adapted extremophile organism capable of surviving and metabolizing in hard vacuum
The spores' exothermic metabolism converts matter directly to heat with extraordinary efficiency—understanding the biochemistry could yield new energy conversion technologies
Dormant spore samples are valuable for xenobiology research and potentially for industrial applications in materials processing
known_incidents: The survey ship Tinder Moth transited the cloud's outer fringe in 2612 and acquired a hull colony that was not detected for 3 weeks; by the time the colony was identified, spore metabolism had corroded through 4 millimeters of hull plating along the ventral surface, requiring emergency drydock repairs.

A xenobiology team aboard the shielded vessel Hearthstone spent 6 months studying the cloud from within in 2625-2626, cataloging over 40 distinct spore morphologies and documenting a complete metabolic activation cycle; their findings confirmed the spores are a single organism—the largest known living thing by volume in the catalogued sector.
description: The Kindling Spore Drift is alive. It is a cloud of biological spores 340,000 kilometers across, drifting through the interstellar medium on a slow elliptical migration that takes millennia to complete. The spores glow. Metabolically active colonies within the cloud produce bioluminescent emissions in the orange-red spectrum, and from a distance the cloud resembles a vast, diffuse field of drifting embers—warm points of light scattered through a haze of organic particulate. Thermal hotspots within the cloud mark regions of intense metabolic activity where spore colonies have found matter to consume, reaching temperatures of 400 to 700 kelvin through purely biological exothermic reactions.

The spores are extremophiles of extraordinary resilience. They survive in hard vacuum, metabolize a wide range of materials including metals and synthetic compounds, and convert consumed matter into heat with an efficiency that borders on the thermodynamically implausible. Dormant spores can remain viable for centuries, activating within minutes of contact with consumable material or sufficient energy input. When active, they glow, they heat, and they consume. Hull plating, sensor housings, cable insulation—the spores are indiscriminate, metabolizing whatever they contact and generating heat as they do so. Mature colonies can corrode through standard hull alloys in weeks, and the thermal output at contact points can weaken surrounding structure further.

The Kindling Spore Drift is estimated to be approximately 400 million years old, based on evolutionary markers in the spore genome. The Hearthstone expedition confirmed that the entire cloud constitutes a single organism—the largest known living thing in the catalogued sector by volume. Individual spore morphologies vary, with over 40 distinct forms documented serving different functions: reproduction, metabolism, structural support, and long-range dispersal via tendrils that shed into space. The organism's evolutionary origin is unclear; no environment in normal space provides the conditions that would select for vacuum-adapted exothermic metabolism on this scale. Some xenobiologists hypothesize that the organism originated on a volcanic world and adapted to space in stages; others suggest it may have arrived from outside the known sector entirely.

The Kindling Spore Drift is classified as a high-danger biological hazard, and its migration path through the sector is tracked and published in navigation advisories updated annually. Ships that must transit the cloud are advised to maintain maximum speed, seal all external ports, and submit to quarantine inspection afterward. The Tinder Moth incident demonstrated that even brief fringe contact can result in hull colonization, and full decontamination requires specialized treatment. Despite the hazards, the organism is of immense scientific value—its metabolic chemistry, if understood and replicated, could provide a biological pathway for direct matter-to-energy conversion. The cloud drifts on through the dark, glowing like scattered coals, the largest living fire in known space, consuming whatever it touches and converting it to warmth with patient, biological indifference.
